headline: Approved $29,500 contract for police chief search; motion to table resolution seeking reopened federal corruption investigation failed 4-4.
summary: A change to annual performance evaluations for council employees passed 7-1. Two Open Meeting Law complaints went to the Legal Department, and grants for a road safety program and bulletproof vests were accepted. Residents also spoke about the Arlington neighborhood sewer project, e-bike safety, and trash pickup.

Approved $29,500 contract with Blue Integrity Consulting for the police chief search, 8-0.

Motion to table the resolution calling for reopening the federal corruption investigation failed, 4-4.

Approved accepting a $27,999.02 Bulletproof Vest Partnership Program award, 8-0.
Approved accepting a $48,759.90 state federal municipal road safety grant, 8-0.
Approved accepting a gift of exercise equipment from Planet Fitness for the Fire Department, 8-0.

METHUEN CITY COUNCIL REGULAR MEETING MINUTES                               
Monday, October 19, 2026 @ 7:00 P.M.   
GREAT HALL, SEARLES BUILDING 
 
1. Roll Call - Members present – Clr. Marsan, Clr. Santos, Clr. Simard, Clr. Valley, 
Clr. DiZoglio, Clr. Drew, Clr. MacLaren and Chair Soto – 1 absent (Clr. Pesce) 
 
2. Acceptance of the Agenda - Motion to accept by Clr. Simard, seconded by Clr. 
DiZoglio – UPON VOTE – Unanimously approved – 8 yes, 1 absent (Clr. Pesce) 
 
3. Pledge of Allegiance/Invocation/Moment of Silence – Chair Soto recognized Clr. 
Santos for the Invocation – Clr. Santos said, “Heavenly Father, we ask for your wisdom 
and guidance as we gather tonight. Bless us with unity, patience, and compassion. May 
our decisions reflect integrity, fairness, and a genuine commitment to serving the people 
of Methuen. Remind us that leadership is a privilege and service is our purpose. In Your 
holy name, we pray. Amen.” Chair Soto recognized Clr. MacLaren, “And let's please 
take a moment of silence for a valuable member of our community, and the late husband 
of the Director of our Senior Center, Susan Riccio, Don Riccio.” 
4. Public Participation: 
Laurie Keegan, 68 Munroe Avenue, Methuen – “Good evening. My name is Laurie Keegan at 
68 Monroe Avenue. I want to preface my statements that while my knowledge of topics comes 
from the conversation with the School Committee Administration and the School 
Administration because of my role on the Finance Subcommittee for the School Committee, I 
do not speak for the School Committee, the Administration, or the Finance Subcommittee. The 
following thoughts are my personal insight and opinions, not that of the School Committee as a 
whole or the district. This evening on the agenda is a question about the school contracts going 
through the city solicitor. I'd like to first thank Chair Soto for bringing this issue to the attention 
of the City Council. Additionally, I want to thank the city procurement office, CAFO and the 
Mayor for working together with the School Department counterparts to resolve the immediate 
issues in the short term to move many of the delayed contracts along in the past week. With 
only a couple of left outstanding seven weeks after the start of the school year. I genuinely 
appreciate the collaboration happening in the past couple of weeks since the finance 
subcommittee met to address the current situation. Given that this is a repeat of last year's 
contract issues, I am hoping that we can all work together to solve the underlying structural 
situation that is causing a delay in school contracts. Recently, an email went out to all 
departments stating that the city Legal Department requires 30 business days to turn around any 
and all contracts. 30 business days equate to six weeks. While this is a perfectly reasonable 
timeline for a municipality, in the context of a 40-week school year, six weeks is 15% of the 
academic school year. If there are any red lines to a contract and it has to go back to a vendor 
for discussion and then needs to go back to legal for approval for another six weeks, that's 30% 
of the school year and so on. This back and forth is directly impacting our students' ability to 
access essential tools for learning. Last year, it was our new literacy program and our advanced 
placement textbooks. This year, it is Infinite Campus and Mac Minis for our marketing and 
television production CTE programs. While the Mac Mini contract was finalized last week, due 
to the delay, we don't expect to receive the shipment until November. The delay in contract also 
caused our price to increase, so we are now paying more for the equipment than we had to. The 
renewal of Infinite Campus contract, our student information management software, was 
delayed such that we could not pay the bill and we had to call and ask for an extension while the 
contracts went through Legal. This contract went to the city on August 14th. It is currently in 
the Legal Department with edits underway. These contracts are burdening our overworked,

GREAT HALL, SEARLES BUILDING 
 
understaffed City Department unnecessarily. I ask that you work with the solicitor, the CAFO, 
the Mayor, and the School Department to find a permanent solution to avoid these bottlenecks 
and unintentionally impacting our students from getting the education they deserve and also 
negatively impacting the running of our school district. While the current crisis is being 
addressed, we need to work together to be proactive in preventing the same situation from 
happening next year when we will have a newly appointed permanent Superintendent in place. 
We want to set the administration up for success with the tools they need to run our district. 
And therefore, I'm hoping we can learn from the past two years and start now in a thoughtful 
and collaborative approach to fix the issue once and for all. Thank you for your time.” 
Dan Shibilia, 22 Riverview Ave, Methuen – “Dan Shabilia, 22 Review Ave. I'm going to start 
with the positive. I do want to commend you guys for the work on the contract issue with the 
schools. It has been an ongoing issue. As Member Keegan just stated, it is something that is long 
overdue, and having someone who can focus on and specialize in the academia contracts is 
going to be a big help to getting things done. So, I do applaud you for that work. I'm not just 
here to be negative. But I do want to focus tonight on the resolution to reopen the investigation. 
And I want to state first and foremost that, Councilman MacLaren, you were right. You can't 
begin to heal until justice has been served. And that hasn't happened yet. The joke of a sentence 
that Solomon got for the crimes he committed in the city and then pled guilty to, the 
embarrassment that was handed down to Sean Fountain after faking being a cop and arresting 
people that we're going to end up having to pay the bill for and then was let to skate. Nothing 
there resembles anything close to justice. So, I wanted to remind this Council that the statement, 
just a piece of paper, was used last meeting. This time last year we were in this room, and it was 
just a piece of paper that was being pushed to admonish the past Superintendent and the School 
Committee. And that was a hill that all of you that were here then were willing to die on. It was 
just a piece of paper used to tarnish the schools and the reputation and relationships. But now 
it's just a piece of paper, and every one of the four of you that voted no, why are you so afraid of 
it? Why is this piece of paper so scary? So, with the public outcry being as visible as it is, and 
how people are desperately seeking closure, I know Councilman Marsan had mentioned in the 
last meeting that the residents he spoke to wanted this to end. I'm hoping that between the 
conversations and the outcry and the people in this room, there are more voices to add to that 
echo chamber, and you have the ability to contemplate any change of opinions. There was also 
a statement made last week that it didn't impact you. So why should we continue this? But it 
did, because don't you pay taxes in this city? Don't you have children in schools? Don't you 
benefit from the roads and the public safety facilities that the city offers that we pay for with tax 
dollars? It’s impacted an entire city. For years, Methuen was dragged through the mud over the 
biggest black eye this community has ever had. We've had our fair share of issues in this city 
over the last 40, 50 years. But it was a national embarrassment on national news. It tore the city 
apart. It eroded trust in the PD. It took another big bite of trust from local government, and it 
cost taxpayers hundreds of thousands of dollars, which most likely we will never get back. That 
money could have been used to save a teacher's job, to benefit our students. It could have 
brought on more DPW workers. There are so many things that that money could have 
benefited, but we were spending it on legal services or inflated pensions. And I know this isn't a 
back and forth, but if the argument's going to be, well, it didn't impact me, why should I have a 
personal connection to it? I hope that during the discussion that can be addressed. Public service 
is a privilege, and we're here to serve the residents. That's what was stated during the invocation. 
You don't get to care only when it touches your friends or your interests. You were elected to do
METHUEN CITY COUNCIL REGULAR MEETING MINUTES                               
Monday, October 19, 2026 @ 7:00 P.M.   
GREAT HALL, SEARLES BUILDING 
 
right by the residents. I know better than most that you can't please everybody, but you need to 
try, even when it's difficult. If you vote no tonight, you're turning your back on this community. 
You're refusing to use every tool in your toolkit, and it's just another reason why people hate 
politics and politicians. If we continue to have these trust issues with Methuen government, it's 
not going to benefit us. So, to any Councilor planning to vote no, look at the residents in this 
room and tell them it doesn't matter. Explain to them why the teachers we can't afford to keep 
and explain to every family that's been embarrassed to say they're from Methuen. It doesn't 
impact me is your standard. That doesn't belong on this table, and maybe you don't belong at 
this table. So, let's not hide behind it doesn't impact me. Don't be self-serving, and remember, it's 
just a piece of paper.”  
Greg Curtis, 23 Hampshire Road, Unit 109, Methuen - Greg Curtis from 23 Hampshire Road, 
Unit 109 in Methuen. I was planning to come tonight and speak with Ryan (DiZolgio), but 
Ryan invited me to say something here. Last Friday afternoon at 5:30, I was taking a pleasant 
walk on the rail trail when I felt a tremendous and painful blow to my lower back. I was being 
assaulted, blindsided, punched in the back. I looked up, and there were six to eight teenagers on 
e-bikes speeding away from the scene. They all had their hoods up. One of them turned around 
and smiled, the one in the red hoodie, at what he had done. He had punched a senior citizen, I'll 
admit, in the back, and they sped off. So, I continued down the path. I decided to reach out and 
warn other people in the path, and some of them had been accosted as well, three ladies. They 
said that the teens were yelling profanities at them and swearing at them, insulting them. Then a 
woman who said that she almost got knocked over by the teens and she was afraid she was 
going to be hurt by the teenagers as they sped by. I tried to speak with a Spanish man. I used 
Google Translate, and nothing happened to him, fortunately. Then I called the police. The 
police came down. It was a wonderful response, two squad cars, and they offered care at the 
scene. There was also some great follow-up today as well. I was down at the station, and the 
camera sort of near the depot, there they were, a nice photograph. So, there's a nice photograph 
that's going to be circulated regarding these teens. I don't know where you're at. I know it's an 
ongoing discussion here in Methuen and across the state about e-bikes and about teens too. As a 
social worker myself and a former director of a nearby school, I think we need to carefully 
consider too what kind of power we're putting into the hands of teenagers. Developmentally, 
teens tend not to be as careful thinkers. They don't think about consequences, and not all. Most 
teenagers are great. But teens like this, I think maybe we need to review some policies. Maybe 
something can be done on a policy level or maybe even more on an enforcement level. I 
certainly don't hold it to the Police that this happened. They can't be everywhere at once. So, 
I'm fine. I just want to be part of the solution. If anybody wants to invite me to be part of the 
solution, I'd be glad to offer my experience, my expertise, and my thoughts about things. But I 
leave any further discussion to your wise counsel. So, thank you very much.”  
Linda Soucy, 10 Kirk Street, Methuen – “Linda Soucy, 10 Kirk Street, Methuen. You'll have 
to let me know when I only have one minute left. I'm just going to read it so that I don't 
misspeak. I sent a letter to the Governor, the State Reps, the Senator, Congresswoman, US 
Senators, Mayors, and community leaders. Let me just start by quoting what Governor Healey 
from her 7-30-2026 press release said. ‘Every family deserves to know that when they turn on 
the tap, they'll have safe, clean drinking water. And every community deserves reliable 
wastewater infrastructure that protects public health in our cities and towns.’ I cannot agree 
with that statement anymore. And if this is what everyone truly believes, then tell me why not

GREAT HALL, SEARLES BUILDING 
 
here in Methuen or in the Arlington Neighborhood of Methuen. I'm reaching out on behalf of 
the residents and the small businesses of the Methuen Arlington Neighborhood to request 
funding to complete the ongoing infrastructure project in the neighborhood. The estimated 
funding needed to complete all four phases is approximately $70 million. In 2024, Methuen 
began the four-phase project expected to cost $100 million to eliminate the combined sewer 
system and replace infrastructure that is more than 150 years old from the 1870s. The project 
will replace existing water and sewer services, address lead concerns, install new drains to 
separate stormwater from the combined sewer system, and eliminate off-street sewer main 
crossings. In my opinion, there has to be lead in the pipes. The EPA says lead service lines that 
were installed primarily from the late 1800s through the 1940s have lead in them. The pipes 
themselves could be lead. Lead service lines were used during that period, particularly in older 
cities, and Methuen, as you know, is 300 years old. Even if the main pipes are copper or iron, 
the system could have lead solder, lead-containing fittings, or brass fixtures. Plumbing installed 
before 1986 is considerably more likely to contain lead, and the fact that the vast majority of the 
homes in our neighborhood were built prior to 1986 solidifies my opinion, my own opinion, 
that there is lead in our pipes. This is not a project waiting to happen. This is a shovel-ready 
project that's already had phase one completed. The combined sewer system in our 
neighborhood is the only one that has not been done for the entire 26 square miles in Methuen. 
You left out 14 streets over the years when these things have been done. My question is why, in 
a low-income neighborhood, would you have left lead pipes in our neighborhood? There are 103 
small businesses in this neighborhood, and according to the U.S. Census, there are over 4,792 
residents that live here. These businesses were already impacted by COVID-19 and have now 
faced additional challenges from phase one construction. Stopping the project before it is 
completed would put residents and businesses in an unacceptable position. We have asked for 
help. Okay, I'll talk faster. We have asked for help. Senator Payano has sought a total of $15 
million in bond earmark funding, of which $5 million has been signed into law but not released. 
The other $10 million is currently in conference committee, and I don't know if that will be 
released. We have reached out to Congresswoman (Trahan), Senator Markey, Senator Warren's 
office. The city has submitted a $35 million state revolving fund request, which has not been 
funded. Again, we have asked. We have submitted. We have been meeting since March of 
2023. Everybody here has been invited. Everybody gets our agendas. Everybody knows what's 
going on. There is lead in our pipes, and we need to figure out how to get the $70 million to 
complete this project. I don't know if you can call the Governor's office. I don't know who you 
have to call. But I look at all the money that keeps coming in to all the surrounding 
communities here, and if you don't think lead in people's pipes are a number one priority and a 
health and safety issue for the residents of our neighborhood, then there shouldn't be anybody 
else funded. That should be the top priority for the State of Massachusetts, and I am beyond 
right now. I'm also just going to leave you the letter that I sent to you on the hookah. I would 
like a moratorium on hookahs in this city. There's no need for these to be popping up in our 
neighborhoods. Thank you.” 
Ruth Estes, 41 Center Street, Methuen - I'm Ruth Estes, 41 Center Street in Methuen. Tonight 
I'm asking for your continued support and urgent action to secure the approximately $70 million 
needed to complete the remaining phases of our neighborhood's water and sewer infrastructure 
project. Our neighborhood is home to nearly 4,800 residents and approximately 103 small 
businesses. It is also the only remaining neighborhood in Methuen where the combined sewer 
system has not yet been eliminated. In 2024, the city began a four-phase $100 million project to

replace infrastructures that dates back more than 150 years. Modernized water and sewer 
services address potential lead concerns and separate stormwater from sanitary sewage. This is a 
public health issue, an environmental issue, and an economic issue. The age of our 
infrastructure raises serious concerns about potential lead exposure, and our outdated sewer 
system contributes to unnecessary wastewater, treatment costs, and the risk of sewer discharges 
into the Merrimack River. Phase 1, funded through ARPA, is nearing completion. Residents 
and businesses have already endured significant construction disruptions. Stopping now could 
lead to critical problems, unresolved, and force our community to face further disruption in the 
future. We have been advocating for this project since March of 2023. Senator Payano, as Linda 
had stated, has sought $15 million in bond earmarked funding, including $5 million signed into 
law, but not yet released, and another $10 million in conference committees and negotiations. 
We have also contacted Congresswoman Lori Trahan and Senator Ed Markey. The city has 
submitted a $35 million state revolving fund requested that remains unfunded. We have 
attended meetings, submitted requests, and continue to advocate. We need a clear path forward. 
Tonight, I respectfully ask the Mayor and City Council to prioritize this project, continue 
pursuing every available state and federal funding opportunity, and help secure the 
approximately $70 million needed to complete the remaining phases. Our residents deserve safe, 
reliable infrastructure. Our small businesses deserve stability, and our community deserves to 
know that this project will be completed. We are not asking for luxury. We are asking for safe 
water, modern sewer infrastructure, environmental protection, and a healthier future for our 
neighborhood. Please help to ensure that the Methuen-Arlington neighborhood does not have to 
wait another century for the infrastructure it deserves. The shovels are already in the ground, so 
let's finish the job.” 
Jade Jalbert, 6 Lady Slipper Lane, Methuen – “Good evening, all. I'm Jade Jalbert, 6 Lady 
Slipper Lane. At your last meeting, four of you voted against TR-26-90, sending a letter to 
reopen an investigation on felon Joseph Solomon and officer impersonator Sean Fountain. I 
hope that you reconsider. I do agree with Councilor Pesce's sentiments from last meeting. This 
letter is not a guarantee that anything will happen. It also does not guarantee an investigation 
will be opened. For the good of those that you represent, make the effort anyway. Councilor 
Soto, you mentioned that this letter would not let the city heal and that it was time to move on. 
This is more than an open wound. This is a disembowelment given the potential legal 
ramifications. Move on with the trail of blood leading right back to us. Leaving this alone is 
allowing the city to bleed out. Doing the right thing would be trying to correct what you can 
correct, not ignoring and pretending it didn't happen. Councilor Marsan, you had mentioned 
that you hadn't heard from the residents. Hopefully my voice, including the two that spoke at 
the last meeting, as well as whomever you've heard from since you made that statement, shows 
that we do care about this. We do want that letter sent. You had also mentioned that you were 
hoodwinked into not reviewing the contract for the second read as you were supposed to so 
many years ago, which helped put us into this mess to begin with. I urge you to seek the 
Solicitor's advice on whether or not your vote is a conflict of interest there. We don't want a 
repeat of that. To the rest of you, this issue matters. It matters to the residents, and it should 
matter to you. Do not make the mistake of voting against it because you think it does not affect 
you personally. I assure you it will. Solomon's claw back, if any is received, will not cover the 
lawsuits we'll face, let alone the deficit we're already working under. Notice I say we. Me, the 
people here, the people at home, and absolutely each and every one of you personally. Show the 
people that you do care about more than yourselves, that you're here representing the residents

of Methuen. Send the letter. Speak for the city. I'm sorry if I'm not engaging enough to keep 
your attention while I'm speaking. So sorry for the intrusion of your time. Speak for the city, not 
yourselves. Thank you.” 
Diane Alaimo, 14 Old Farm Road, Methuen – “I'm Diana Alaimo, 14 Old Farm Road. This is 
short. I just want to thank you, Mayor Beauregard, for requesting that this corruption case be 
reopened. And thank you to the five Councilors who signed the letter in support of the Mayor. 
I'm very surprised and disappointed that support for this request was not unanimous, and that 
both councilors representing my district are among the four who did not stand in support of the 
mayor. I'm at a loss for why the support was not unanimous, but I'm hopeful that the second 
reading of this letter will allow the Councilors to stand in support as a matter of integrity. This 
corruption case is a stain on our community, and most residents were blindsided during all 
phases of the investigation. Thank you, Mayor, for drafting a comprehensive letter outlining the 
many layers of this case, and for bringing to light the community leaders who have fought hard 
to obtain justice for my fellow residents. Thank you.”

9. Presentations/Projects/Department Updates - Veterans Service Officer Jordan  
Normandia Presentation of 90 Days in Review – Chair Soto recognized Clr. Simard, “Thank 
you, Madam Chair. We planned on having a Subcommittee meeting on this, but since Mr. 
Normandia is our new Director, he's been in office for 90 days, I figured it would be a bigger 
audience if he came before the full Council, give us kind of a narrative of what he's been doing 
the last 90 days, talk about upcoming events, and then field any questions we may have as our 
new VSO. So, I'll give the floor to Mr. Normandia. Thank you for coming, Jordan.” VSO 
Jordan Normandia said, “Good evening, Mayor, Madam Chair, members of the City Council.

GREAT HALL, SEARLES BUILDING 
 
Thank you for having me tonight. So, I just want to provide an update on my first 90 days as the 
new VSO here since starting in July. So, my focus has been on three main things, serving the 
veterans and their families, the community, strengthening the actual administration day-to-day 
of the existing programs that the office works with, and making our services more accessible 
throughout the community. So just a quick glance. I've assisted with approximately 17 VA or 
other benefit-related claims and matters, so those are either things that are filed, pending, or 
various statuses, so those are hard claims. The next thing that my office mainly deals with is 
Chapter 115, so that caseload currently stands at 20 active cases. There's about a little more than 
that that are either recurring, closed, various different statuses, but active we have 20 cases 
throughout the city here. And I roughly – it's hard to kind of give you a number, but I have a lot 
of walk-ins and e-mails, phone calls, things like that, so roughly since I started I have about 90 
to 100 in-person visits with more, like I said, not in-person things like phone calls and e-mails 
and the like. For Chapter 115, I reviewed our existing recipient files, conducted our semi-annual 
recertifications, followed up on missing paperwork, eligibility concerns, and other requirements 
that are required for that benefit program, and we've processed a few new applications, but 
mostly it's just been recertification. And I've also worked on improving our documentation 
procedure for that, kind of worked to standardize it a little bit more. So going through the 
numbers quickly, for Chapter 115, roughly from July through September, we've had benefits 
paid around $43,000, and that kind of goes broken up month to month there. And for those of 
you not familiar with it, it's a program for veterans that kind of need a little bit more financial 
assistance, and it is something that the state does reimburse us back through. So, we pay – the 
state reimburses about 75%, and then we cover the rest. So that's just a rough estimate. Out of 
that $43,000, we get back $32,000, and the $11,000 would come out of our pocket there. And 
that's just a real rough estimate. So, benefits and constituent assistance, so I've helped veterans 
with, like I said, disability claims, rating increases, obtaining certain records, including like their 
medical records or just service records, awards, and also help them kind of understanding 
benefit decisions and kind of seeing the path for whether it needs to be escalated to a higher level 
review or get the rating increased, different things like that. Also help with annuities, property
